noticias.titulo: Kuwait reports drone attacks as Iran, US trade attacks on Qeshm and Bahrain
noticias.resumen: Kuwait's military says its air defence was repelling drones as Iran and the US hit out at each other across the Gulf.
noticias.texto:
Kuwait reports drone attacks as Iran, US trade attacks on Qeshm and Bahrain
Iran claims drone strike on US radar was retaliation for alleged airspace violations by US military drones.
Kuwait’s army has said the Gulf country is under attack by drones while the United States and Iran traded blows, marking escalating tensions in the region as a peace deal remains elusive.
The military said in a statement on X on Tuesday that “any explosion sounds heard are the result of air defence systems intercepting hostile attacks”.
The US earlier carried out several attacks on Iran’s southern island of Qeshm, in the Strait of Hormuz, hours after Iran said it launched a drone attack on a US radar system in Bahrain.
“The American attack on locations on Qeshm island caused no damage to residential, commercial, or infrastructural areas,” Ahmad Nafisi, deputy governor of Iran’s southern Hormozgan province, told the official IRNA news agency on Tuesday.
He said the situation was under control and relief agencies were on full alert. IRNA reported five to six explosions on the island on Tuesday evening.
A US official told Al Jazeera the strike hit a missile launch site on Qeshm, in response to Iran’s earlier attack on a US base in Bahrain.
US Central Command said Iranian drones aimed at a US radar system at an air base in Bahrain “were intercepted without any damage to US equipment or personnel”.
Bahrain attack
Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said it carried out a “precision operation” with drones on the US-operated radar at the Sheikh Isa air base, in response to “repeated violations of Iranian airspace by US military drones”.
Bahrain, which hosts the US Navy’s Fifth Fleet, said its air defences intercepted the attack, and blasts were heard over the capital, Manama, according to the AFP news agency.
It was the third Iranian drone attack on Bahrain in five days after a lull of several weeks. Friday’s strike was the first Iranian attack on a Gulf country since early September, AFP reported. Reuters said it came after a Bahraini court sentenced 64 people, mostly Shia clerics, to life in prison for allegedly colluding with Iran.
Kuwait’s armed forces said on Tuesday night that its air defences were responding to “hostile drone attacks” and urged the public to follow safety instructions.
It did not say where the drones came from or whether there were casualties or damage.
Tankers hit in Hormuz
Iran’s armed forces said three oil tankers struck naval mines while trying to cross the strait on Tuesday. The US military says it cleared the main routes of mines.
Since the war began on February 28, Iran has tried to restrict traffic through the strait, which normally carries about a fifth of the world’s oil, insisting that ships use only routes it has authorised. The US has responded with a naval blockade of Iranian ports and has escorted tankers.
Another tanker, the Panamanian-flagged Tara Gas, was struck on Monday about seven nautical miles north of Khasab, in Oman, causing a fire in its engine room, according to the security firm Vanguard.
Vanguard and India’s ports minister initially said all 25 crew, 24 of them Indian, were safe. But the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations agency said the vessel was hit a second time and the crew were “currently unaccounted for”. India’s ports minister later said the crew had abandoned the vessel after a second attack and that one Indian sailor was missing. Another Panamanian-flagged tanker, the On Phoenix, was hit by an unidentified projectile off Oman’s coast on Monday.
Ongoing diplomacy
Iran’s foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, and his Omani counterpart, Badr Albusaidi, discussed safeguarding shipping and diplomatic options in Muscat, Oman’s news agencies said.
A third US aircraft carrier, the USS Theodore Roosevelt, arrived in the Middle East on Monday, and US President Donald Trump is due to hold a three-way summit on Thursday in China with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin, where the Iran war is on the agenda.

noticias.titulo: Israel parliament elects Gadi Eisenkot ally Matan Kahana as new speaker
noticias.resumen: Eisenkot’s bloc has pledged to undo some of Netanyahu’s most contentious domestic policies following Kahana’s election.
noticias.texto:
Israel parliament elects Gadi Eisenkot ally Matan Kahana as new speaker
Eisenkot’s bloc has pledged to undo some of Netanyahu’s most contentious policies following Kahana’s election.
Israeli lawmakers have elected Matan Kahana as the new parliament speaker, marking a step towards reversing domestic policies from the outgoing government led by Benjamin Netanyahu.
Kahana, an ally of Gadi Eisenkot – the party leader currently working to form the next government and replace Netanyahu – was voted in on Tuesday, receiving 66 votes in the 120-member chamber.
Netanyahu’s Likud party had put forward Ofir Katz as its own candidate. He received 52 votes following a stormy debate that stretched over seven hours.
The Israel parliament speaker is an important office given that it sets the timetable for parliamentary business and can therefore speed up or delay debates or votes on proposed legislation.
“I will be a Knesset speaker for everyone, irrespective of race, religion or gender,” said Kahana during his inauguration speech immediately after the vote.
Kahana, a 54-year-old former special forces soldier, is expected as soon as Wednesday to start the process of undoing much of Netanyahu’s domestic agenda, especially regarding contentious reforms to the judiciary.
Netanyahu is Israel’s longest-serving prime minister, having been in and out of office for three decades.
The vote took place weeks after October 27 parliamentary elections in which neither Eisenkot nor Netanyahu won a majority in the Knesset, with the two blocs trading barbs since then.
Eisenkot’s wide-ranging bloc secured 48 seats, while Netanyahu’s finished with 53. Two Arab-majority slates won an unprecedented 19 seats on the back of anger over Netanyahu’s hard-right government.
On Tuesday, the two lists voted for Eisenkot’s candidate Kahana as parliament speaker, with one Arab Knesset member absent.
Netanyahu’s and Eisenkot’s parties met on Sunday to discuss the possibility of joining a unity government but the meeting appeared to be largely a formality, with both men saying they should be prime minister.
Netanyahu, who has reportedly been urging US President Donald Trump to resume the war on Iran, has talked up the threat from Tehran as he insists on the need for a unity government.
Sweeping reforms
With Kahana at the helm and if Eisenkot retains the backing of the Arab-Israeli parties, he has an opportunity to deal serious blows to Netanyahu’s legislative agenda even before a possible government is formed.
Eisenkot has said he wants to rescind sweeping reforms to reduce the independence of the judiciary that were advanced by Netanyahu, who has been enraged over corruption charges against him that could land him in prison if he loses power.
Eisenkot has also vowed to quickly set up a state commission of inquiry to investigate security failures that led to Hamas’s October 7, 2023 attack.
Netanyahu, who has built his brand on saying he will ensure Israel’s security, has refused an independent probe, instead proposing one whose members would be chosen by politicians.
Kahana, who is now a member of Eisenkot’s Yashar party, served in a short-lived non-Netanyahu government in 2021 and 2022 as minister for religious services, during which he clashed with ultra-Orthodox Jews by seeking to reduce the power of the Chief Rabbinate.
Kahana himself is an observant Jew, part of Eisenkot’s efforts to form a broad coalition that ranges from secular liberals to religious conservatives.
As parliament speaker, Kahana succeeds Amir Ohana, a Netanyahu ally who has held the position since 2022.

noticias.titulo: Haitians protest in support of El Salvador’s anti-gang troop deployment
noticias.resumen: El Salvador's security minister has confirmed the troops will leave once kidnapped technicians are rescued.
noticias.texto:
Haitians protest in support of El Salvador’s anti-gang troop deployment
El Salvador’s security minister has confirmed the troops will leave once kidnapped technicians are rescued.
Demonstrators have marched in several Haitian cities to show support for a deployment of troops from El Salvador, despite concerns that the outside intervention may worsen instability in the Caribbean country.
On Tuesday, hundreds of protesters rallied in the streets of cities like the capital, Port-au-Prince, bearing signs with slogans like “Down with the gangs”.
Haiti has long struggled with gang violence, but the crisis worsened around 2021, after the assassination of President Jovenel Moise. His death further weakened Haiti’s central government, and experts say gangs took advantage of the eroding public confidence to expand their influence.
The October 18 kidnapping of four Salvadoran aviation technicians near Port-au-Prince prompted El Salvador’s President Nayib Bukele to respond with a military operation to Haiti.
But on Monday, El Salvador confirmed it would end its deployment of about 2,500 troops once the missing Salvadoran airmen were found.
“If they reappear tomorrow, as President Bukele said, we will leave,” Salvadoran Security Minister Gustavo Villatoro said.
That announcement, however, was followed by public gestures of support and diplomatic engagements, with some top officials in Haiti encouraging the Salvadoran deployment to stay.
Haitian Justice Minister Patrick Pelissier travelled to San Salvador on Monday and expressed gratitude for the troop surge.
“The Haitian people applaud the decision of Nayib Bukele to send troops,” Pelissier said on Monday.
He added that Haitian security forces, together with their international counterparts, had recently managed to regain control of Haiti’s national football stadium, held by gangs for years.
“During the operation, we discovered several human skulls inside the stadium,” Bukele claimed in a social media post last week.
A ‘mano dura’ approach
The timeline for the Salvadoran troop withdrawal is uncertain. While El Salvador has framed its deployment as a rescue mission, the leader of Haiti’s 400 Mawozo gang, Wilson Joseph, told The Associated Press that the four technicians are already dead.
Joseph added that the abduction took place in territory controlled by Chen Mechan, a rival gang. He provided no evidence to back his assertions.
Bukele, however, has championed his country’s role in confronting Haiti’s gangs, using social media to promote the offensive and sharing videos of military operations.
The Salvadoran president — who once referred to himself as the “world’s coolest dictator” — has been credited with popularising a “mano dura” or “strong hand” approach to regional security.
Faced with one of the highest homicide rates in the world, Bukele launched a hardline security crackdown on gangs in El Salvador in 2022, including mass arrests and mass trials.
His heavy-handed approach has led to a sharp decline in crime but has also been widely condemned for human rights abuses.
Critics have warned that transplanting such tactics to Haiti could spark a backlash, leading to greater instability and risks to civilians.
They have also criticised the lack of long-term planning for El Salvador’s troop deployment; a sudden withdrawal, for instance, could worsen the situation for Haiti’s security forces.
Bukele is campaigning for a third term in El Salvador’s February presidential election, and analysts speculate his actions in Haiti could be used as a campaign tool to drum up support.
A series of international actions
The Salvadoran deployment is the latest in a series of international interventions in Haiti.
Such foreign involvement is often controversial. The United States, for instance, has sent troops to Haiti on multiple occasions in the 20th century, occupying the country for decades and seizing control of its central bank.
More recently, a United Nations-backed Gang Suppression Force (GSF) arrived in Haiti in April, to help address the widespread gang violence.
Gangs control more than 80 percent of the capital region. The conflict has killed more than 22,000 people since 2022. UN reports attribute more than half of the deaths in the first nine months of the year to security operations, including the deaths of 300 civilians.
The UN also says almost 2,000 people have been displaced since the arrival of Salvadoran troops.
But Pelissier said Haiti’s government had not reported any civilian casualties in the latest operations, which he described as professional.
“The best to do is to avoid, as much as possible, human rights violations, and that’s what we are doing together,” the minister said.

noticias.titulo: Russian military plane crash in Siberia kills 19
noticias.resumen: Russia's Defence Ministry says preliminary findings for the crash point to equipment failure.
noticias.texto:
Russian military plane crash in Siberia kills 19
Russia’s Defence Ministry says preliminary findings on the crash point to equipment failure.
A military plane has crashed in western Siberia, killing all 19 people on board, according to a statement from the Russian Defence Ministry, cited by local media.
The Antonov An-12 transport aircraft went down in an unpopulated area near the city of Kemerovo, about 3,000km east of Moscow. The An-12 typically has a crew of six.
Air force experts were investigating the cause of the crash, but preliminary findings pointed to equipment failure.
“A commission from the Russian Aerospace Forces is working at the site to establish all the circumstances of the incident,” the ministry’s statement was quoted as saying by the RIA Novosti news agency.
Regional Governor Ilya Seredyuk, posting on Telegram from the scene of the accident, said emergency crews had extinguished a fire. He said crews were helping to investigate the accident.
Seredyuk, in a video posted online showing the site of the accident near the village of Yagunovo, said the plane had been flying through the region when it crashed.
The Investigative Committee, Russia’s top criminal investigation agency, launched an inquiry into possible violations of flight safety rules, a standard practice following crashes.
The An-12 is a Soviet-built four-engine turboprop transport plane that has been in service since the late 1950s. More than 1,000 were built, and some still remain in operation in Russia and other nations.
In September, a Russian Tupolev Tu-95 military aircraft crashed in the eastern region of Amur, killing six crew members and injuring a seventh.

noticias.titulo: US Fed’s Lisa Cook refuses to attend White House hearing
noticias.resumen: US President Donald Trump has been trying to fire Cook since August 2025.
noticias.texto:
US Fed’s Lisa Cook refuses to attend White House hearing
US President Donald Trump has been trying to fire Cook since August 2025.
United States Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook has declined, through her lawyers, to appear next month before a Trump administration committee that is considering whether she should be fired, calling the process unfair and committed to a predetermined outcome.
The refusal extends the wrangling between the White House and Cook’s lawyers regarding her appearance before the committee, which the administration of US President Donald Trump initially demanded for November 6.
Administration officials have called on Cook to appear before the committee to address allegations that she committed mortgage fraud in 2021, before she joined the Fed’s board of governors, a charge she denies. Cook has not been charged with any crime.
Trump has sought to fire Cook since August 2025, and she has argued that the president’s efforts to do so represent a threat to the Fed’s independence and reflect Trump’s desire to force the central bank to reduce borrowing costs.
“Governor Cook has no legal obligation to participate in an unfair hearing — and indeed, has a duty to the Federal Reserve to decline to participate in any proceeding that would undermine the institution’s unique status and independence,” Abbe David Lowell, Cook’s lawyer, wrote in a letter released on Tuesday to White House counsel William Scharf. The three-person panel set up by the White House to consider the allegations “appears to be a facade designed to obscure a predetermined decision to fire Governor Cook”, the letter said.
In June, the US Supreme Court blocked Trump from removing Cook while litigation over the attempted firing continues, finding that “the fact of independence but also the appearance of independence is key to the Federal Reserve’s design”.
Trump officials have threatened to move ahead with the hearing even without Cook, and in a November 3 letter said that the three-member committee “reserves the right to draw adverse inferences against you” for not participating.
The unusual “committee of inquiry” set up by the White House consists of Kevin Hassett, Trump’s top economic adviser; Andrea Lucas, whom Trump appointed to lead the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission; and Keith Sonderling, Trump’s pick for Department of Labor secretary.
The Supreme Court said in a footnote to its June ruling that Trump could try again to fire Cook if the administration provided her adequate notice and an opportunity to respond. The committee of inquiry is an effort to meet those conditions.
Under the law governing the Fed, the president can only fire a Fed governor “for cause”, but the Supreme Court didn’t address whether Cook’s actions met that standard. The committee will ultimately recommend whether there is cause to fire Cook, the White House has said.

noticias.titulo: UK hands NATO-assigned US soldier accused of Russia spying to US military
noticias.resumen: UK authorities have passed the investigation to the US 'in line with existing international protocols'.
noticias.texto:
UK hands NATO-assigned US soldier accused of Russia spying to US military
United Kingdom authorities have passed the investigation to the United States ‘in line with existing international protocols’.
A senior United States soldier assigned to NATO who was arrested in Britain last week on suspicion of spying for Russia has been transferred to US military custody, United Kingdom police have said.
The Head of Counter Terrorism Police (CTP), Assistant Commissioner Laurence Taylor, said on Tuesday that authorities in London have passed the investigation to US partners “in line with existing international protocols”.
The 41-year-old man was arrested by British police on November 10 near Gloucester on suspicion of offences under Section 1 and Section 3 of the UK National Security Act 2023.
Section 1 relates to obtaining or disclosing protected information, while Section 3 relates to assisting a foreign intelligence service.
“These are extremely serious allegations, and our collective response should send a strong message that we will act swiftly and robustly where we suspect this kind of espionage activity taking place,” Taylor said.
He added, “We will continue to support our US colleagues as they take the matter forwards.”
US FBI Director Kash Patel said the army officer is in US custody as a “result of an espionage investigation” between the FBI’s Philadelphia field office and Legat London in addition to partners at “UK Counter Terrorism Policing, MI5, UK Defence Counter Intelligence, and the US Army Counterintelligence Command.”
Brigadier General Sean Stinchon, the commanding general of US Army Counterintelligence Command (ACIC), said the case illustrated the “remarkable partnership” between ACIC, US Army prosecutors, the FBI, the US Department of Justice, and the UK.
Stinchon added that this example sends a “stark warning to any service member suspected of violating the oath”.
The case is believed to be the first time a US soldier was found to be under suspicion of spying for a foreign government while in the UK.

noticias.titulo: ‘Zero transparency’: Inside Trump’s plans for Venezuela’s oil money
noticias.resumen: Democrats say they plan to investigate Trump's dealings with Venezuela after winning control of Congress.
noticias.texto:
‘Zero transparency’: Inside Trump’s plans for Venezuela’s oil money
Democrats say they plan to investigate Trump’s dealings with Venezuela after winning control of Congress.
The administration of United States President Donald Trump is facing criticism over how it has handled billions of dollars in oil revenue collected from Venezuela.
Since January 3, Trump’s government has controlled Venezuela’s oil exports, gathering the revenue in an account overseen exclusively by the US Treasury.
Last week, the Department of State released a 53-page report aimed at shedding light on the account’s activities. It revealed that at least $12.11bn have passed through the account since the start of the year.
But critics say the report lacks key details about where the money came from and who it is going to.
“There’s been zero transparency on all of the financial engineering associated with how $12bn of Venezuelan oil was changing hands and being utilised,” said Tyson Slocum, the director of the energy programme at Public Citizen, a US-based consumer advocacy nonprofit.
“All we have now is a very barebones narrative of how the funds were used, but not details on what entities were involved.”
Questions of sovereignty
Concerns about Trump’s plans for Venezuela’s oil sector began late last year, when his government began seizing oil tankers leaving the South American country.
Any oil on board, Trump said, would be kept or sold by the US. He and members of his administration framed the confiscated fuel as compensation for the losses incurred when Venezuela nationalised its oil industry decades ago.
“American sweat, ingenuity and toil created the oil industry in Venezuela,” White House aide Stephen Miller said at the time. “Its tyrannical expropriation was the largest recorded theft of American wealth and property.”
Tensions between the US and Venezuela reached a tipping point on January 3, when Trump authorised a military operation to abduct Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro.
In a speech that morning, Trump highlighted the role oil had played in his decision. “We’re going to be taking out a tremendous amount of wealth out of the ground,” Trump said.
He proceeded to explain that some of the Venezuelan oil proceeds would go “to the United States of America in the form of reimbursement for the damages caused us by that country”.
Days later, Trump revealed he had spoken to oil companies “before and after” the operation. He also held a meeting with oil industry executives at the White House to discuss plans for Venezuela.
Legal experts have raised concerns that the January 3 operation was an attack on Venezuela’s sovereignty, in violation of international law.
They have also questioned the legality of seizing another country’s natural resources, given that a 1962 United Nations resolution grants nations “permanent sovereignty” over their own natural resources.
But supporters of Trump’s actions have pointed to Maduro’s history of violent repression and anti-democratic actions in Venezuela as justification for the operation.
Maduro has since been replaced by his former vice president, Delcy Rodriguez, who has largely cooperated with Trump’s demands.
But the focus on Venezuela’s oil revenue has left some critics questioning whether Trump plans to address the human rights issues in the South American country.
Trump has repeatedly downplayed the importance of democratic elections in Venezuela, said John Feeley, a former US ambassador and senior diplomat in Latin America.
“Trump has made patently clear that he has no interest in the democratic future of Venezuela,” said Feeley, calling the US-Venezuela relationship “protectorate neocolonialism”.
‘The biggest oil deal in history’
More recent manoeuvres have also raised speculation about the Trump administration’s commitment to transparency in its management of Venezuelan oil.
In late August, for instance, Trump announced his government would have a direct stake in extracting nearly a fifth of Venezuela’s oil.
Under the terms of the agreement, the US gained “majority control” in a 100-year deal for 17 Venezuelan oilfields, with proven reserves of 65 billion barrels.
North American Blue Energy Partners (NABEP), a company owned by Venezuelan businessman Alejandro Betancourt, was given the rights to operate the fields.
The Pentagon, meanwhile, took a 35 percent stake in the company, and the US was guaranteed 20 percent of the oil output at cost. Trump called it “the biggest oil deal in history”.
But Betancourt has faced investigations in the US, Spain and Switzerland over accusations of money laundering.
After this article was published, a spokesperson for NABEP reached out to Al Jazeera with a statement that Betancourt “has never been charged with a crime in any country and denies wrongdoing”.
Venezuelan opposition leader Maria Corina Machado, however, said the contract with NABEP “evidently does not reflect the levels of transparency that Venezuelan society wants”.
Venezuela has long struggled to export its oil, so the fact that it will now be sold on the open market is beneficial to the country’s economy, said Luis A Pacheco, a former executive with Venezuela’s state oil company and nonresident fellow at the Baker Institute Center for Energy Studies at Rice University.
But Pacheco is sceptical of Trump’s deal with NABEP.
“This is an obscure outfit with no known financial sources, with very little tech wherewithal,” he said. “This so-called mega-deal, without doubt, will certainly yield very little of what’s expected of it.”
Little transparency over billions of dollars
The shroud of secrecy surrounding the Venezuelan oil deals has spurred some Democrats in the US Congress to press for greater accountability.
In September, Democrats in the House of Representatives (PDF) and Senate asked the administration to disclose what had been uncovered by KPMG, an outside accounting firm hired to audit transactions involving Venezuelan oil exports.
The State Department did issue its report last week. But key portions were redacted, including who deposited money into the accounts and who the final recipients of the funds were.
Feeley, the diplomat, said there are also questions about the total sum of the proceeds. Only $12bn is accounted for in the report.
“We have no idea how that money was used, and we have no idea what percent of the total amount of money deposited in the US Treasury that $12bn represents,” said Feeley. “But most experts allege that it is only a fraction.”
In a statement to Al Jazeera, a State Department spokesperson said its report “provides a comprehensive account, down to the cent, of the Venezuelan natural resource revenues deposited in, held by, and disbursed” from the account.
Venezuela’s requests for disbursement are checked against a “list of approved and prohibited expenditure categories”, the spokesperson added.
The funds are then used for “essential public services, macroeconomic stability, and the rebuilding of key sectors such as energy, healthcare and infrastructure”.
But who receives those funds remains unclear. Pacheco said there is no reason the US could not disclose details of the monetary flow.
“Even though this report gives you some information, it still doesn’t give you light into the most important thing, which is what is the Venezuelan regime is doing with the money,” Pacheco said.
“You can affirm with very good certainty, when you talk about billions of dollars, something is draining away.”
Pacheco also questioned the supervisory role the Trump administration has claimed over the Venezuelan government. At one point, Trump even claimed he would “run” the South American country.
“The discourse of the White House is that they exert some sort of tutelage over the Venezuelan regime,” Pacheco said. “But apparently that tutelage doesn’t go as far as to tell the Venezuelans where is the money going to.”
New Congress, new oversight?
But this year’s midterm elections could usher in a wave of oversight into the Venezuelan oil money.
Democrats won majority control in both the House and Senate in the November 3 midterm elections, and lawmakers have already floated the possibility of opening investigations, once the new Congress arrives in January.
“The admin is sending billions to Delcy Rodriguez’s corrupt government where the list of who benefits is kept murky,” Representative Joaquin Castro wrote on social media after the election.
“I will continue to demand answers, and use every tool we will have with the incoming Democratic majority, including congressional hearings, to uncover what the United States is doing in Venezuela.”
One area of exploration might be the role private oil trading companies play in the Trump administration’s deal. Firms like Vitol, a Dutch multinational energy company, could be put under the microscope.
A week before Trump sent troops into Caracas to abduct Maduro, John Addison, a senior trader with Vitol, held a secret meeting with Vice President JD Vance on a tarmac in Montana, according to the news agency Reuters.
Vitol was later able to buy oil from the state-owned Venezuelan oil company at a steep discount. Addison and his wife donated $6m to Trump’s election campaign in 2024.
Democrats on the House Oversight Committee have long been eager to investigate the dealings of firms like Vitol in Venezuela.
“Oversight Democrats will not stop until we know exactly what companies are profiting from these foreign policy decisions, especially in Venezuela,” Representative Robert Garcia said in January.
Garcia is expected to chair the oversight committee next year.

noticias.titulo: Five EU states announce plans for immigration ‘return hubs’ in Rwanda
noticias.resumen: Germany, Austria, Netherlands, Denmark and Greece likely to face challenges to policy criticised as ‘grave moral failing’ Five EU member states have announced plans to set up an offshore centre in Rwanda for people with no legal right to stay in Europe, in a pilot scheme that is expected to face legal challenges and has been denounced as “a grave moral failing”. noticias.texto:
Five EU member states have announced plans to set up an offshore centre in Rwanda for people with no legal right to stay in Europe, in a pilot scheme that is expected to face legal challenges and has been denounced as “a grave moral failing”.
The five countries – Germany, Austria, the Netherlands, Denmark and Greece – are the first to seek to use the EU’s newly agreed returns law that allows people who have exhausted all avenues of appeal against their removal from Europe to be sent to a third country.
In a statement released on Monday the five EU countries said “concrete negotiations with partner country Rwanda will begin for implementation”, saying the scheme would make “an important contribution to further curbing illegal migration, dismantling the business model of smugglers and relieving the burden on our population”.
Officials hope to send 100 people to Rwanda from early next year to test the model. The scheme will apply to adults whose claims to asylum have been rejected or others with no legal right to live in the EU.
In theory, according to diplomatic sources, migrants would stay in a reception centre in Rwanda for a couple of months, before choosing to integrate into life in the Great Lakes country or return to their home nation.
Unlike the failed scheme pursued by the British Conservative government in Rwanda, or Italy’s agreement with Albania, it will not apply to people pursuing asylum claims.
The reception centre, which would be an open facility, was not intended to house people long term but to accommodate regular flows of people, the countries said. Diplomatic sources said the EU countries were not using British-funded facilities built in Kigali.
The governments involved argue it will protect the European asylum system while removing the incentive for irregular migrants to come to Europe.
Denmark’s immigration minister, Morten Bødskov, whose government has pioneered a tough line on migration widely emulated across the EU, said it was “a huge breakthrough”.
The German interior minister, Alexander Dobrindt, said: “Return hubs offer a positive approach for people without the right to stay and with no prospects in Europe, whose countries of origin do not cooperate in the repatriation process.”
Andy Burnham told reporters last week that the UK had not had direct discussions with European governments involved in return hubs but “we will watch that with interest, learning from what went on in the past. The public want us to do whatever we can to deal with illegal immigration.”
Critics have highlighted the ethical difficulties of striking an agreement with Rwanda’s repressive government, which was found in 2024 by the US state department to allow state security forces and civilian officials to commit human rights abuses with impunity, while also raising concerns about freedom of expression and forced labour.
Spain’s socialist prime minister, Pedro Sanchez, said on Monday the move had no “future or humanity”. “I don’t see any future or humanity in that. It’s not the solution,” Sanchez, an outspoken defender of immigration in a Europe that has tilted to the right in recent years, told Telecinco television.
The French Green MEP Mélissa Camara denounced the agreement between the five countries and Rwanda as “an agreement of shame” and “a grave moral failing”. She said: “Under this agreement, people will be deported thousands of kilometres away from the European Union, with no guarantees regarding the compliance with their rights.”
Alain Berset, the secretary general of the Council of Europe, the continent’s human rights body, said it was not possible “to be so precise a priori” about what any return hubs proposal meant. Speaking to the Guardian before the announcement, he said all members of the Council of Europe were committed to the European convention on human rights “and this must be the lighthouse” for all discussions on return hubs.
“On concrete cases, then we will have to see if this is compliant with the convention,” he said. He stressed that “all countries must be able to define their migration policy”.
Officials involved in setting up the migration centres expect legal challenges, but say the scheme is grounded in human rights law.
Rights organisations say the scheme is bound to fail. “Member states may call them ‘return hubs’ or even ‘welcome centres’, but no euphemism can hide the violence of uprooting people from the life they’ve been building in Europe, and sending them to a country they don’t even know, without family, networks or meaningful prospects,” said Chiara Catelli of Picum, a pan-European organisation that campaigns for the rights of undocumented migrants.

Nigeria’s National Drug Law Enforcement Agency (NDLEA) said a 28-year-old player named as Greene Da’monte Khiree from the state of Georgia was arrested at Lagos’s main airport last Wednesday after he arrived on a flight from Thailand via the United Arab Emirates. noticias.texto:
An American basketball player has been arrested in Nigeria for allegedly attempting to smuggle 33.95kg (75lb) of marijuana into the country.
Nigeria’s National Drug Law Enforcement Agency (NDLEA) said a 28-year-old player named as Greene Da’monte Khiree from the state of Georgia was arrested at Lagos’s main airport last Wednesday after he arrived on a flight from Thailand via the United Arab Emirates.
The NDLEA said the player told them he had come to Nigeria to “build networks” for his basketball career. The agency said evidence on his phone suggested he had “knowledge of and involvement in the drug trafficking activity”. The NDLEA said it detained the player when he attempted to leave the airport with his hand luggage after abandoning two checked-in bags. The agency said those two bags were found to contain 32 parcels of marijuana, and a tracking device.
Nigeria has strict drug laws, and trafficking carries a sentence of life in prison.
A basketball player by the name of Damonte Greene is listed on the roster of the Pattani Raptors in the Thai Premier Men’s League. Greene, a Georgia native, played college basketball for Reinhardt University and South Georgia Technical College. He played semi-professional basketball in the US before representing a number of teams in Thailand.
WNBA star Brittney Griner and former Utah State player Jarred Shaw were imprisoned in Russia and Indonesia respectively for marijuana offenses. Griner was released in December 2022, while Shaw remains in prison.

noticias.titulo: Relocation of Cape Town baboons to sanctuary ignites heated protests
noticias.resumen: Demonstrators tried to block vehicle carrying the baboons, whose capture authorities say is needed to protect both primate and human The relocation of a troop of baboons in Cape Town to a wildlife sanctuary has triggered furious protests by local people opposed to their capture, which officials argue is necessary to stop human-wildlife conflict in the city. The 44-member Waterfall troop (named after the area they mainly inhabit) was captured in the southern seaside suburb of Simon’s Town on Friday and Saturday. A second, smaller Seaforth troop is also due to be moved. Continue reading...
noticias.texto:
The relocation of a troop of baboons in Cape Town to a wildlife sanctuary has triggered furious protests by local people opposed to their capture, which officials argue is necessary to stop human-wildlife conflict in the city.
The 44-member Waterfall troop (named after the area they mainly inhabit) was captured in the southern seaside suburb of Simon’s Town on Friday and Saturday. A second, smaller Seaforth troop is also due to be moved.
The growth in both baboon and human populations in Cape Town in recent years has led to increased conflict and more baboons dying as a result. Meanwhile, a heated debate has raged between people who believe that baboons and humans can coexist and those who argue that baboons in urban areas are in danger and in some cases need to be relocated. Some animal rights activists have compared authorities’ baboon management to apartheid.
During Friday’s relocation, outraged protesters tried to stop vehicles taking the baboons away. One person sprayed a fire extinguisher, according to the Daily Maverick, a local news outlet.
After the confrontation, the local Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals branch urged those opposed to the baboons’ capture not to try to stop the vehicles. “Capture and transport are already stressful for the baboons,” it said in a statement. “Delaying their arrival prolongs their time in crates and risks adding to that stress – this is not fair on the baboons.”
It said it remained opposed to the baboon’s relocation, adding: “Our presence did not imply support … our inspectors are present because the animals need someone looking out for them.”
On Sunday, dozens of people sat outside the wildlife centre in a silent protest, some tying flowers to the fence. Baboons from a different troop also gathered at the boundary, calling to the newly captive animals, the Daily Maverick reported.
“We stand together for the Seaforth and Waterfall troops, for their freedom, their dignity and their right to live as wild animals,” Mandy Neal, the administrator of the Save Kogelfontein Baboons Facebook group, posted on Monday, calling for weekly Sunday silent protests. “ Our message is simple: CAPTIVITY IS NOT CONSERVATION.”
The City of Cape Town said in a statement on Sunday that the relocation had been successful, with the baboons being monitored 24/7 after being checked by vets and the females receiving contraceptive implants.
It said: “The Waterfall troop has been relocated due to the severity and persistence of human-baboon conflict in the Simon’s Town urban environment, the limited available natural low-lying habitat, the increasing risk to the baboons’ welfare, and public safety concerns … [and] as a very last resort after other interventions were evaluated and deemed ineffective, and as an alternative to culling.”
Prof Justin O’Riain, a behavioural ecologist at the University of Cape Town, said the baboon management plan had undergone two years of public consultations. “It has thus been disappointing watching members of the public and select NGOs, many which did not engage in the stakeholder process, now compromising the safety and welfare of the baboons and people through violent actions directed at staff and baboons in transit.”

noticias.titulo: Caribbean nations fear economic impact of shuttering citizenship program after EU threats
noticias.resumen: St Kitts and Nevis to wind down citizenship-by-investment program after EU warns of end to visa-free access The decision by St Kitts and Nevis to end a lucrative programme offering citizenship to wealthy foreigners in exchange for investment threatens its economy and ability to support people in need, the premier of the island of Nevis has warned. On Friday, Terrance Drew, the prime minister of the twin-island Caribbean nation, announced he would wind down the citizenship-by-investment (CBI) programme, after the European Union threatened to end visa-free access for St Kitts and Nevis. Continue
noticias.texto:
The decision by St Kitts and Nevis to end a lucrative programme offering citizenship to wealthy foreigners in exchange for investment threatens its economy and ability to support people in need, the premier of the island of Nevis has warned.
On Friday, Terrance Drew, the prime minister of the twin-island Caribbean nation, announced he would wind down the citizenship-by-investment (CBI) programme, after the European Union threatened to end visa-free access for St Kitts and Nevis.
Mark Brantley, the premier of Nevis, which has autonomous self-governance in some aspects, said he understood that the “country was given very little choice”, but did not “support the winding down of the program”.
The 42-year-old CBI programme, which St Kitts and Nevis pioneered, allows wealthy foreigners to obtain citizenship and ultimately a passport by investing in infrastructure and other development projects. It has brought billions of dollars into the country and in some years accounted for the largest share of government revenue.
In June, the European Commission wrote to the five Caribbean nations that currently operate CBI programmes: St Kitts and Nevis, Dominica, Antigua and Barbuda, Grenada and St Lucia. It warned that countries may lose visa-free access to its 29-country Schengen area if they did not phase out CBI.
In Friday’s statement, Drew blamed concerns over the programme on mismanagement by previous administrations, including years of underselling to undercut other countries, a controversial prison project, weak escrow protections and investment sums not being properly paid into the citizenship unit.
He said his government had led major reforms to the Caribbean’s programmes with international partners, including the US treasury, but argued that continuing the programme risked visa-free travel to parts of Europe and access to international banking. That could disrupt services allowing visitors to use overseas cards and families abroad to send money home.
Brantley, however, argued it was unfair for the EU to force St Kitts and Nevis to make a move without offering assistance to navigate the transition to other industries.
“I have not yet seen from the EU any corresponding suggestions of assistance. And we have to realise that these citizenship-by-investment programs, not only in St Kitts and Nevis, but … smaller countries of the Caribbean, have contributed significantly to our gross domestic product and also to ensuring that our people … can get adequate access to water and to education, to healthcare and the like,” he said.
Brantley described the 1 June 2028 deadline the EU gave the country to phase out the lucrative programme as “frankly ludicrous”.
In his statement, Drew said the CBI programme “did a lot of good, but it also created a danger”.
“When one source pays for half or more of everything, you are at its mercy. If it stops, everything stops. That is putting all of your eggs in one basket,” he added.
The prime minister said the government aimed to diversify its economy by strengthening tourism, yachting, and digital and creative industries, among others. He added that the sale of clean, geothermal energy was “at the heart of it” with drilling and exploration already planned.
“I will not pretend that the road is easy. Less CBI money means we must spend wisely and plan carefully. We will. Our plan is to make this change by growing our economy. Raising taxes is not part of that plan,” Drew said.
Antigua and Barbuda has also expressed willingness to end the programme, though it is trying to negotiate a longer transition period. The five Caribbean governments have taken differing positions on the EU demand. According to local media, Grenada has indicated it wants its programme to continue until 2032, while Dominica and St Lucia have responded to Brussels without publicly committing to ending their programmes.
Jermine Abel in Basseterre contributed reporting

noticias.titulo: Isolated Brazilian tribe emerges amid alarm over threats to group’s way of life
noticias.resumen: Indigenous Awá people of Amazon make contact with villagers and accept food to take back to territory About 20 Indigenous people emerged from isolation in Brazil’s Amazon rainforest, several organizations reported on Tuesday, raising the alarm about increased invasions into the tribe’s territory. According to the NGO Survival International, members of the Awá people, who live in voluntary isolation, arrived on Monday in a village and made contact with a government team in a “historic encounter”. Continue reading...
noticias.texto:
About 20 Indigenous people emerged from isolation in Brazil’s Amazon rainforest, several organizations reported on Tuesday, raising the alarm about increased invasions into the tribe’s territory.
According to the NGO Survival International, members of the Awá people, who live in voluntary isolation, arrived on Monday in a village and made contact with a government team in a “historic encounter”.
The village they entered was within the Arariboia Indigenous territory in the north-eastern state of Maranhão, home to the Guajajara ethnic group.
Local community leaders said the villagers offered food to the group.
“They asked for yams and took them back into their forest,” said Survival International.
The NGO explained that the Awá typically subsist on hunting and gathering. However, they have faced increased incursions from illegal loggers, hunters and cattle ranchers.
A video of the encounter, filmed by Guajajara villagers and released by Survival International, shows a group of men, women and children at the edge of the forest.
Partially concealed by vegetation, they appear naked and are wearing necklaces. The men carry bows and long arrows.
“The physical condition of some members, particularly the children and the elderly, caused concern among the villagers, who noted clear signs of severe emaciation,” warned Coapima, an organization representing Indigenous groups in Maranhão.
Coapima highlighted the risks that unplanned contact poses to such groups, noting that they are particularly “exposed to diseases” against which they have little to no immunity.
Funai, the public agency responsible for Indigenous affairs, said in a statement sent to AFP that its technical teams were closely monitoring the situation and analyzing available information regarding the group’s health.
Survival International’s director, Caroline Pearce, said the group’s choice to emerge from isolation was a “troubling indication of how the continued invasion of uncontacted peoples’ forests puts otherwise self-sufficient Indigenous people in real danger”.
She said the Awá were being driven into “an ever-smaller island of the Amazon rainforest, surrounded by destruction”.
According to the NGO, about 196 “uncontacted” peoples and groups, who choose to live in isolation, have been identified across 10 countries.
More than 90% of such groups live in the Amazon rainforest, primarily in Brazil, with others in Indonesia and India.
The Forest Guardians – a group of Guajajara people who have battled illegal invasions for years – warned in comments in the Survival International statement that “climate change, fires, deforestation and land encroachment” were affecting the Awá’s way of life.
According to Survival International, many of the guardians have lost their lives trying to protect the territory they share with the Awá.

noticias.titulo: Eight-year-old Haitian boy returns home after release from ICE custody
noticias.resumen: Child reunited with family after he was detained by immigration agents in San Diego and transferred to Texas An eight-year-old Haitian boy who was put into restraints and detained by immigration agents in San Diego on 4 November and transferred to a facility in Texas has been reunited with his family in California . Representative Juan Vargas shared a photograph of the boy and his family in a social media post on Monda, writing: “11 days ago, an 8-year-old in San Diego was taken into federal custody during an immigration check-in. He was separated from his loved ones and held in a facility in
noticias.texto:
An eight-year-old Haitian boy who was put into restraints and detained by immigration agents in San Diego on 4 November and transferred to a facility in Texas has been reunited with his family in California.
Representative Juan Vargas shared a photograph of the boy and his family in a social media post on Monda, writing: “11 days ago, an 8-year-old in San Diego was taken into federal custody during an immigration check-in. He was separated from his loved ones and held in a facility in Texas. Today, he’s finally home.”
The Haitian Bridge Alliance, an immigration advocacy group, confirmed that the third-grader had been released from Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) custody.
“An eight-year-old child belongs in a classroom, on a playground, and surrounded by love – not in immigration detention. We welcome his release, but his freedom should never have required a public outcry,” Guerline Jozef, executive director of the Haitian Bridge Alliance, said in a statement.
The third-grader at Fay elementary school was put in restraints and taken into custody by federal immigration officers at a check-in earlier in the month, according to video obtained by NBC News and an oversight letter Democratic lawmakers sent to the Departments of Homeland Security and Health and Human Services.
A spokesperson for the homeland security department said ICE took the child into custody “out of an abundance of caution and to ensure the child’s safety”.
The uncle, the spokesperson said in a statement to the Guardian, was unable to prove legal guardianship – and that officials were obliged by federal anti-trafficking laws to take the boy into care as an “unaccompanied alien child”.
The Haitian Bridge Alliance said the boy was in the care of his uncle and cousins after his father was deported last year.
“I’m so grateful that he’s home, but this should have never happened in the first place,” Vargas said in a second social media post, adding that he would be asking the Trump administration for answers. While he was detained, the child was “held in a facility in Texas, far away from his home in San Diego”, Vargas said.
Celebrating the boy’s return, Jozef of the Haitian Bridge Alliance told NBC News: “The aunt was literally crying, and she said: ‘I have not eaten since the Wednesday they took my baby.’ They haven’t been able to sleep because of that.” She added: “The cousins were there when they took him, and wondering: will they ever see him again? But today [Monday] they are able to see him again. They are able to hug him.”

noticias.titulo: Sleeve checks and no smartglasses: South Korea races to protect all-important university exams against AI
noticias.resumen: South Korea has been gripped by revelations of AI-aided cheating, just days before more than half a million students are to sit high-stakes entrance exams The integrity of South Korea’s career-defining university entrance exam has been thrown into doubt after the top scorer in a recent professional exam admitted using a concealed camera and AI to cheat.
